articles.title: David and Louise Matchett exchanged more than 1,400 letters while he served overseas in World War II; their daughter later gave the collection to a local historical society
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of David and Louise Matchett, who exchanged over 1,400 love letters during World War II, documenting their enduring love and everyday life amid the chaos of war.
articles.body: During World War II, many individuals were separated from loved ones due to the deployment of soldiers to overseas territories. Writing letters became one of the ways through which individuals could share news and exchange affection with each other. For newlyweds, David and Louise Matchett, these letters became a vital component in their marital life. The couple’s correspondence started in 1942 and went on through most of the war period to capture their thoughts and experiences of the separation.David and Louise had both been raised in the South Side of Chicago. David had been working as a practicing lawyer while Louise had started her bachelor’s degree at the University of Chicago before they got married in 1942. Within three weeks after getting married, David had enlisted for military service at Fort Sheridan, Illinois. Most of the war period, he spent time overseas while Louise stayed in the United States. From July 1942 through October 1944, the couple exchanged more than 1,400 letters. This communication ultimately formed a private account of their marriage and daily activities during World War II. Their daughter, Mary Kingery and husband, Daniel, donated this collection to the Winnetka Historical Society many years later. The Winnetka Historical Society wrote about this love story in its Spring 2011 Gazette under the heading “Matchett Letters Open Door on WWII Love Story,” written by Susan Crowe Whitcomb.A marriage interrupted by military serviceBoth David and Louise grew up on the South Side of Chicago. They were children of influential people in the city. David’s father was a judge on the Cook County Appellate Court, while Louise’s father was the principal of Fenger High School. The Gazette says that when they married in 1942, David was a practicing attorney and Louise was finishing her bachelor's degree at the University of Chicago. Soon after the couple's marriage, David left for his military service at Fort Sheridan.According to the Gazette, David was attached to the Army Medical Corps for most of the war, much of it in Papua, New Guinea. While he did not fight himself, David saw the impact of the war on injured soldiers who came to the hospital where he was stationed. The earlier letters were filled with the reasons why he thought the US was at war. Later, military regulations prevented him from disclosing details about his location and movements to Louise in case the letters were to fall into the wrong hands. In a letter to Louise dated January 19 44, David explained that he could not say where he was and where he was going to go because even he did not know that. These restrictions left her with limited information about his surroundings, but their correspondence continued.How V-Mail helped them stay connectedLetters were an important part of communication between military personnel and their families during World War II. The Winnetka Historical Society’s account explains that correspondence helped maintain morale among soldiers overseas and encouraged support for the effort at home. According to the Gazette, the Matchetts were fond of using V-Mails, which were introduced in 1942 through collaboration of the US Post Office and the War and Navy Departments. V-Mails were meant to minimise the amount of space required to ship large amounts of overseas mail.The messages were written on the sheets of paper provided by the Post Office. The letters were taken to the processing centre, where they were opened, censored and photographed on microfilm. This film was shipped overseas, where the messages were printed and delivered to their destinations. The Matchetts made use of this service frequently. Louise wrote almost daily, filling her V-Mail sheets with stories about what was going on at home and talk of their future life together. Their letters talked about their friends who died during the war or were shot down while fighting above enemy lines.‘Prince’ and ‘Snow White’While there were instances when David was asked about his military duties and his views on various news reports, their love towards one another constituted the main focus of their correspondence. For instance, Louise always called David her ‘Prince,’ and he used to call her ‘Snow White’. The couple sent each other messages about their life together, expectations for the future and dreams of the day when they would reunite. In one of their letters written in March 1944, Louise assured David that he was still the most important man in her life. Moreover, she stated that she always prayed for his good health and success, and wished that he would return as quickly as possible. He responded to her in the same way. In one of the letters sent in the same month, David stated that seeing Louise after disembarkation in the United States would be the happiest event after their wedding. At the end of his letter, he told Louise that he loved her with all his heart and nothing could ever come between them.The letter became part of a historical collectionDavid came back to the United States during late 1944 for Judge Advocate General Officer Candidate School in Ann Arbor, Michigan. He continued his career in the JAG Corps up until 1946. In the 1950s, David and Louise moved from Chicago to Northfield, Illinois and lived there along with their daughter, Mary. David died in 1974, whereas Louise died in 2011. Their daughter, Mary Kingery and her husband, Daniel, donated the letters to the Winnetka Historical Society. The collection consisted of over 1,400 letters that were written from July 1942 to October 1944. The historical society’s account of the collection offers a personal view of World War II, beyond military records and official reports. The letters document the restrictions placed on overseas correspondence, the role of V-Mail and the everyday concerns of a couple separated by military service. What started as a way for two newlyweds to stay connected became an invaluable historical document. In the words of Louise and David themselves, future generations will get to know their story, their aspirations and the fears of living in the midst of a worldwide war.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran carries out flogging of singer who performed without a hijab
articles.summary: An Iranian singer and four members of her production team have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online,” an Iranian human rights group and a news website said on Monday.
articles.body: An Iranian singer and four members of her production team have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online,” an Iranian human rights group and a news website said on Monday. Parastoo Ahmadi and the four others were also handed two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and travel, Iran Human Rights and the Emtedad website quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili as saying. The case followed the release of a video on YouTube in December 2024 showing Ahmadi performing without the mandatory hijab alongside male musicians in Qom, south of the capital Tehran, Norway-based human rights group Hengaw said. Western governments and human rights groups have criticized flogging as torture and a violation of international law. Iran rejects accusations over its human rights record, saying Western countries should focus on their own human rights problems. Iranian authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Reuters. Rules requiring women to wear the hijab were a flashpoint during protests in 2022 after the death in custody of Kurdish Iranian woman Mahsa Amini, who was arrested for allegedly violating the dress code. The rules have increasingly been flouted on the streets of Tehran and beyond, and enforcement of the rules has also become more selective.

articles.title: Anne O'Connor: Opposition leaders seek clarity over HSE chief's sacking
articles.summary: Anne O'Connor, who took up her role as HSE chief executive in March, says she will challenge her removal "as vigorously as possible".
articles.body:
Opposition leaders in the Republic of Ireland have called for greater clarity following the removal of HSE (Health Service Executive) Chief Executive Anne O'Connor from her position.

O'Connor was appointed as chief executive of the HSE in December 2025 and started the role in March of this year.

Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin is expected to address O'Connor's sacking in the Dáil (Irish lower of parliament) later on Tuesday.

Irish Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill has stressed the decision to remove O'Connor was exclusively a matter for members of the HSE board. She said they are independent but have her support.

MacNeill confirmed that the HSE board's final decision was communicated to her on Saturday, but that she could not "speak to the reasons that the board made their decision", Irish broadcaster RTÉ has reported.

She thanked O'Connor for her many years of work in the health service, and said she was "a dedicated public servant".

O'Connor has said she will challenge her removal "as vigorously as possible" and "pursue every avenue available to me to vindicate my position and to protect my professional reputation".

She said she did not resign or voluntarily stand down.

The Green Party has called for time to be set aside for a special Dáil debate on the matter.

Independent Ireland said its general secretary Richard O'Donoghue had raised serious concerns about the HSE chief executive's performance in the Dáil last week, questioning her probationary period and asking who was responsible for overseeing it.

It is calling for the Irish government coalition to clarify who knew what and when about O'Connor's departure.

The Irish Hospital Consultants Association has called on the HSE board to resign.

In a statement, the HSE said its board decided to end O'Connor's tenure as it was believed "to be in the best interests of the future operation of the organisation".

"The board would like to thank Anne for her service as CEO and for her many years in senior roles across the health service before that including as Chief Operations Officer throughout the Covid pandemic," the HSE added.

"Deputy Chief Executive Officer, Damien McCallion, has agreed to act as Chief Executive Officer in the interim pending the appointment of a new CEO."

articles.title: Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
articles.summary: South Korean authorities issue air raid warnings after several Russian jets were on verge of entering its airspace.
articles.body:
South Korea has scrambled fighter jets and issued brief air raid warnings for residents of an island after Russian military planes approached its airspace over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.

Russian jets on Tuesday briefly entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone (ADIZ), an aerial buffer area between countries, South Korea’s military said, adding that “multiple” Russian aircraft were “on the verge” of entering the country’s ⁠airspace over Ulleung Island.

“Airspace intrusion was anticipated. Therefore, to protect the safety of our people, we issued a warning pre-emptively,” Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said.

Authorities had earlier issued an alert that a North Korean plane had made an incursion, which would have been a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war after the 1950-1953 Korean War ended with an armistice and not a peace treaty. South Korea later issued a correction saying no North Korean jet was involved.

Here’s everything we know about the incident:

Why did South Korea tell residents to take shelter?

According to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, about five Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s ADIZ on Tuesday morning. There was no intrusion of South Korea’s airspace by the Russian aircraft in the end, the South Korean military said.

Jang said the aircraft came “very close” to the airspace above Ulleung Island, which is home to 9,000 people and lies 120km (75 miles) off the northeastern coast of South Korea. South Korean fighter jets conducted “tactical manoeuvres” to prevent any incident, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

But confusion ensued over the alert and who was responsible for the intrusion.

The government of North Gyeongsang province, which includes Ulleung, sent out an alert saying the jets were suspected to be North Korean, which it later corrected.

Still, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety issued the shelter warning at 7:52am (22:52 GMT on Monday) and lifted the alert three minutes later after the aircraft had left the area.

The last time the island in the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, was sent into panic was in 2022 after North Korea fired more than 20 missiles into the sea during a period of heightened inter-Korean tensions. After one missile headed towards Ulleung, it triggered air raid sirens and led to residents evacuating.

South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it had conveyed its regret over the incident to Russia and called for measures to prevent a recurrence, South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency reported.

The ministry also sent the message to the Russian embassy in Seoul but stopped short of summoning the Russian ambassador, diplomatic sources told the agency.

Still, the Ministry of National Defence called in Russia’s military attache, Nikolai Marchenko, to lodge a formal complaint.

Russian military aircraft have entered South Korea’s ADIZ five times so far this year.

Last week, South Korea announced Russian military aircraft had temporarily entered the ADIZ.

On the same day, Japan protested to Moscow after also saying two suspected Russian aircraft had entered its airspace off its southwestern coast.

In 2019, South Korean fighter jets had fired warning shots after a Russian A-50 early warning aircraft, flying alongside Russian and Chinese bombers in a joint patrol, entered its territorial airspace near the island of Dokdo.

At the time, Moscow denied violating South Korean airspace.

What has Russia said about the incident?

Russia does not recognise South Korea’s authority over its ADIZ and has argued it has no basis in international law.

What is the status of Russian-South Korean relations?

The two countries have fairly strained relations.

Moscow has a close relationship with North Korea, and Pyongyang deployed troops to help Russia’s soldiers during its war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Seoul has joined Western sanctions against Russia due to its invasion of Ukraine.

However, recently, the leaders of the two countries have signalled interest in restoring ties.

Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a 10-minute meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and agreed to pursue cooperation where possible while also working to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula, an official in Seoul told reporters on the condition of anonymity, Yonhap reported.

articles.title: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
articles.summary: Birmingham has more than 34,000 people living in Supported Exempt Accommodation.
articles.body:
The government has announced an independent inquiry into allegations rogue landlords in Birmingham are making huge profits by exploiting a housing scheme.

BBC Panorama reported last month that some companies in the city were taking advantage of the Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) system, intended to provide housing along with care and support for vulnerable people.

There have been claims of fraud, crime, poor housing and firms receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but not giving them the support they are meant to.

A government spokesperson said an eight-week investigation would begin immediately, with initial findings and recommendations reported to ministers in the new year.

Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.

The government added the investigation would examine the scale of the problems in the city's SEA sector, including the quality of accommodation and support, use of public money, and effectiveness of oversight and regulation.

In a letter confirming the appointment, housing secretary Angela Rayner asked Pearson to lead a "rapid independent investigation" into the claims.

She said the investigation should focus on Birmingham, given consistent reports that the area was at the "epicentre of concerns" about poor-quality supported accommodation, while considering the extent to which any findings can be applied to the rest of the country.

"Good-quality supported housing can turn lives around and provide people with the support they need to live as independently as possible," Rayner wrote.

"There are increasing reports, however, that this system is being abused, with vulnerable people exploited at the expense of the taxpayer."

SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse.

In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them .

Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than £200 a week at the time for every person they house.

The council paid out £404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further £211.8m paid between April and July 2026.

More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.

The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties .

Birmingham's Conservatives have welcomed the latest announcement, but they warn the review must not become another excuse to delay reforms already known to be needed to protect vulnerable residents.

It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.

An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.

That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.

Tuesday's announcement follows a recent letter to the prime minister from councillors Robert Alden and Ken Wood, demanding urgent intervention.

Campaigners have called for action for years, under both Conservative and Labour governments.

Alden, the councillor for Erdington and leader of the Birmingham Conservative Group, said it was right that the government examines "why Birmingham has become the epicentre of this crisis and what must change".

"Residents deserve answers about how this was allowed to happen.

"Vulnerable people placed in badly run accommodation deserve proper support, and neighbourhoods suffering the consequences deserve action."

Charities, residents and politicians told Panorama last month that parts of the system were being exploited.

The programme found property agents drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos offering free rooms, PlayStation consoles and holidays.

Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex, said many vulnerable people were being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords".

Alysha told Panorama that she had moved into SEA 18 months ago, a survivor of domestic abuse.

She had nowhere to go and no family living nearby, so she was made homeless and relying on universal credit.

"I never thought I'd be homeless and I never thought my marriage would break down, but it did," she said.

"I felt extremely alone. I needed help getting myself back on to my feet, and that's how I got myself into supported accommodation."

She has since lived in three different SEA properties but admitted her experience was far from the fresh start she needed.

Alysha was forced to leave her first placement after just six months.

"There was one day at about 05:30 in the morning, where I was woken up to screaming and growling and banging.

"They'd been fighting really badly. The house was covered in blood, police were called, and the house was no longer safe."

Her second SEA initially looked "amazing" with brand new kitchen appliances and mattresses but Alysha quickly learnt it was not as it appeared.

Managed by a private provider, Alysha said she was promised weekly counselling sessions, access to food banks, and help with GPs.

"But it's not the case, it's not the case at all," she said.

"They're not interested, they come and they just want you to sign that paper to say Alysha's done support this week and that's it."

She added that the home had been left without heating at one point in the winter.

Jane and Melvin, residents living in Selly Oak, said the house next door to them was converted into SEA.

The couple admit at times they felt unsafe in their own home with the tenants of the property having involvement with guns, knives, and drugs.

"There were people overdosing," Jane recalled, adding: "Twice the front door was kicked in by people who didn't live there."

Melvin said: "Ambulances would pull up with their blue lights flashing at two or three o'clock of a morning.

"There were people running up and down screaming, fights going on... there was one episode where one afternoon the chap was being chased by someone with a knife.

"If he hadn't have been athletic, he'd have been killed."

Jane said she and her husband never objected to the property being used to support people in need.

But she felt as though those living in the SEA were left to run "amuck".

"I think they were lacking the support that they needed, really," she explained.

articles.title: A New York worker fell while cleaning siding from a rental building's roof after leaving his safety harness at home, but judges said the landlord still had to provide protection and upheld a liability ruling against him
articles.summary: A New York appeals court upheld a liability ruling against a landlord after a worker fell from the roof while cleaning siding without his safety harness, emphasizing the landlord's responsibility to provide fall protection.
articles.body: A New York landlord has been held liable after a worker fell from the roof of a rental property while cleaning its exterior siding, even though he had left his personal safety harness at home. An appeals court ruled that the property owner was responsible for providing proper fall protection and could not avoid liability by blaming the worker's decision to proceed without his own equipment.The ruling was upheld by the Appellate Division of the New York State Supreme Court, which affirmed an earlier decision granting partial summary judgment to the injured worker, Benjamin E. Irwin, under the state's Labor Law Section 240(1).Irwin was cleaning vinyl siding on a rental building owned by the defendant when he fell from its roof. He was not using any safety equipment at the time of the accident.The landlord challenged the liability ruling, arguing that the work amounted to routine maintenance and therefore did not qualify for protection under the state law. He also maintained that Irwin's own actions were responsible for the accident because he had left his personal safety harness at home.The appeals court rejected both arguments, finding that the cleaning work involved risks similar to those encountered at construction sites and fell within the protection offered by Section 240(1).Why the court held the landlord responsibleUnder New York's Labor Law Section 240(1), property owners and contractors must provide appropriate safety equipment to protect workers undertaking jobs involving elevation-related hazards.The court noted that although ordinary household window cleaning is generally excluded from the law, other cleaning activities can qualify when they involve comparable risks to construction work.Referring to an earlier ruling in Soto v J. Crew Inc., the judges said cleaning projects must be assessed according to their circumstances, rather than automatically being classified as routine maintenance.In Irwin's case, the court found that the landlord had failed to provide any safety devices despite the risk involved in working at height. It also noted that the property contained at least three rental units, making the owner subject to the statutory safety obligations.The judges said the landlord could not transfer that responsibility to the worker simply because he had chosen to use his own equipment.They also rejected the argument that Irwin should have cleaned the difficult-to-reach sections from second-floor windows instead of climbing onto the roof.The court explained that choosing one method of completing a job over another, even when a safer alternative might have been available, amounts to comparative negligence. That alone does not remove an owner's liability under Section 240(1).The judges found that this defence could not succeed because the landlord had not supplied any safety devices in the first place.Landlord's attempt to recover damages from worker rejectedThe property owner also sought permission to amend his legal response to bring a counterclaim seeking common-law indemnification from Irwin. In effect, he wanted to recover compensation from the injured worker for the liability imposed on him.The appeals court rejected that request, finding that the proposed counterclaim lacked legal merit.The judges said allowing a property owner to recover damages from an injured worker on the basis of that worker's alleged negligence would undermine the purpose of Section 240(1), which provides special protection to people working at elevated locations.The decision also referred to earlier cases establishing that a worker's contributory negligence cannot be used as a defence against liability under the provision.The court unanimously affirmed the lower court's September 18 last year order, which had granted Irwin partial summary judgment on liability and rejected the landlord's request to pursue an indemnification claim.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.
articles.body:
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not new, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutscher Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary."

Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit.

Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".

Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation .

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: Betsi Cadwaladr: Targets and money more important than care - report finds
articles.summary: A review finds targets and money being prioritised over patient care at Betsi Cadwaladr health board.
articles.body:
Wales' largest health board is still failing, with "fundamental weaknesses" in governance and management, a new report says.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has been in special measures for nine years in total, with the latest period starting in 2023.

A review of its leadership published on Tuesday found, in some parts, targets and money "have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".

Committed staff and ability to deliver some strong local services were highlighted.

The review did not suggest splitting up the health board, but Wales' health minister said the findings were "unacceptable" and BCUHB "does not function as a single coherent organisation".

The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer , after it gave Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUHB) a "final chance" to improve.

It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.

The report said: "Many areas reported a culture where targets and financial matters have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care.

"Fear of speaking up was described often... staff did not believe that raising a concern would result in corrective action.

"Despite this, the panel witnessed many teams striving to deliver the very best care they could for patients."

The reviewers also found a "toxic" culture at the health board where staff were afraid to speak out, and worried that no-one would listen if they did.

The health board's chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, previously announced she would be leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.

Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.

The report also said that bureaucracy and slow decision-making led to a "loss of local ownership" and staff feeling frustrated.

The reviewers wrote: "Staff and leaders described decisions moving through multiple layers of approval, authority becoming concentrated at senior levels and operational leaders lacking sufficient autonomy to act.

"A phrase used in a focus group characterised the resulting complexity as 'Betsi spaghetti'."

However, the review concluded the health board could still be improved without being broken up into smaller organisations - an option previously discussed by ministers.

It said staff were "loyal and committed", and there were "strong local services" and "significant clinical expertise across north Wales".

Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor, said "these failings are utterly unacceptable".

"I also share the understandable frustrations of staff and patients alike in north Wales at the lack of progress in delivering and embedding improvements to services and standards of care," he said.

"The report identifies that the health board does not currently demonstrate the organisational conditions required to deliver and sustain reliable improvement.

"It does not function as a single coherent organisation and board governance is immature, impacting on the health board's capability to discharge its accountabilities adequately."

Ap Gwynfor is due to make a statement in the Senedd addressing the report on Tuesday afternoon.

Benjamin Hodge Mckenna MS, Reform UK Wales's health spokesperson, said BCUHB had been "plagued by mismanagement, poor performance and repeated failures".

"Senior leaders and government ministers cannot continue to preside over failure without facing consequences," he said.

Darren Millar MS, leader of the Welsh Conservatives, said: "These damning findings are sadly nothing new.

"Putting the health board in special measures was supposed to improve performance, yet things have got worse and people are dying as a result."

articles.title: Gloucester Airbnb host catches dozens having party on smart doorbell
articles.summary: A homeowner says he is considering ending short lets after a booking turned into a party allegedly attended by up to 80 people.
articles.body:
An Airbnb host says he is considering ending holiday lets after a booking for four guests turned into a party allegedly attended by up to 80 people.

Owner Alex Negrescu said blood was found on the walls and carpets were damaged at his house in Gloucester. It has left him questioning the future of the business despite earning about £20,000 in the past six months.

Negrescu said his smart doorbell alerted him to a large number of people arriving at the property on Saturday, with up to 80 people there by the time he arrived, including an unconscious man.

An Airbnb spokesperson said "disruptive parties are banned" on the platform and confirmed the guest has been suspended for three years.

Gloucestershire Constabulary said officers were called by South Western Ambulance Service at about 20:30 GMT following reports of an unconscious man.

Ambulance crews reported difficulties reaching the property due to large numbers of people in the street blocking access.

Podsmead Road, where the Airbnb is based, was closed by police for about 45 minutes while emergency services dealt with the incident and people left the property.

Negrescu said after reviewing his smart doorbell footage and seeing more than 20 people entering the property, he immediately contacted Airbnb, which agreed to cancel the booking and gave guests 30 minutes to leave.

He said all of the "expensive items of furniture" in the property, such as his TVs, had been piled into one of the bedrooms.

The homeowner, who has invested £300,000 into the property, is now considering switching from short to long-term rentals over fears a similar situation could happen again.

"We've never had issues like this before," he said. "Imagine if I hadn't gone around to the property.

"There could've been hundreds of people there.

"I feel disrespected as a property owner."

An Airbnb spokesperson said they were "disappointed" to hear of this host's experience and have been in touch to offer support.

"While issues on Airbnb are exceptionally rare, our dedicated 24/7 Neighbour Support line allows anyone with concerns about a listing to contact us at any time and we investigate all reports received," they added.

The spokesperson added that Airbnb's Host Damage Protection scheme provides reimbursement of up to $3m (£2,299,095) if a guest causes damage and does not pay for repairs.

articles.title: Ian Huntley murderer gets new whole life term for prison killing
articles.summary: Triple killer Anthony Russell admits murdering child killer Ian Huntley at Frankland Prison.
articles.body:
A triple murderer who beat the notorious child-killer Ian Huntley to death in prison has been given a second whole life jail term.

Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly bludgeoned Huntley, 52, with a metal bar at the high security Frankland Prison near Durham in February, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

Russell, who was jailed for life with no chance of parole in March 2022 for raping and murdering a pregnant woman and killing a mother and son in the West Midlands, admitted Huntley's murder on the second day of his trial.

Sentencing him for what prosecutors called a "cold-blooded" and planned attack , Mr Justice Hilliard KC said Russell would never be freed from prison or eligible for parole.

Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

He and Russell, from Coventry, were both on A-wing and there was "tension" between the killers, the trial had heard.

At about 09:00 GMT on 26 February, Russell attacked Huntley in the prison's recycling workshop, repeatedly beating him about the head with a metal bar.

As a "natural lifer" who would never get parole, Russell said he had "nothing to lose" and intended to murder Huntley, with the attack planned for several weeks, the court heard.

Huntley died nine days later at Newcastle's Royal Victoria Infirmary from unsurvivable brain and skull injuries.

Two incidents showing "tension" between Huntley and Russell had been recorded in Frankland's logs.

In March 2025 the pair were separated while arguing and shouting threats at each other.

In January, weeks before Huntley's murder, Russell was seen with a black eye which prison guards believed might have been caused by the Soham child-killer.

After the fatal attack, in which Huntley sustained at least six blows to the head with the metal bar, Russell told prison staff: "Hopefully I've killed him."

He said he "caved" Huntley's head in as he was "sick" of the murderer, who had been "getting in my face the last few weeks".

Russell had admitted manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility, claiming he was hearing voices and under the influence of childhood post-traumatic stress disorder when he attacked Huntley.

But at the start of the second day of his trial, after prosecutors had opened the case, he changed his plea to murder.

Ahead of sentencing, prosecutor Matthew Bean KC told the court Russell was serving a whole life term for three murders which he admitted committing.

On 21 October 2020, at his flat in Coventry , Russell beat and strangled David Williams, 32, out of "jealousy" due to the mistaken belief the victim had slept with Russell's girlfriend.

Having concealed the body, Russell took his victim's phone and messaged his mother, Julie Williams, in a bid to make her think her son was alive, the court heard.

Three days later he went to the 58-year-old's flat in Coventry and strangled her because he knew she suspected he had murdered her son.

To evade arrest he went to the Leamington Spa area where he met and befriended Nicole McGregor, 31, who was five months pregnant, the court heard.

Hours after meeting her on 26 October 2020, he raped and murdered her, Bean said, to stop her reporting what he had done.

The murderer accepted the killing of Huntley was "deliberate and planned", his barrister Tyrone Smith KC said.

Russell told prison staff Huntley was a "horrible narcissistic person" who "walks around the wing like he's something big and hard and special", Smith said.

Russell felt Huntley was protected by prison guards because of "how high profile" he was, the court heard, and the child-killer had been even more "arrogant" and "cocky" since Russell walked away from an earlier argument.

He told guards he had "nothing to lose" and was "never getting out", so wanted to do the job of murdering Huntley "properly", the court heard.

Smith said Russell was "frank" in expressing "no remorse" towards Huntley, but he apologised to those who witnessed the attack and had to deal with the aftermath.

Hilliard said it was "hardly surprising" there would be tension between two such murderers, telling Russell: "I'm sure you were able to give as good as you got."

He said the "background of antagonism" was the reason for the killing but it in no way reduced the sentence in a case of "exceptionally high seriousness".

articles.title: Prince William meets Burnham on first Downing Street visit
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales is meeting Andy Burnham with homelessness expected to be among the topics.
articles.body:
The Prince of Wales walked up Downing Street for the first time, as he visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Behind the black door of No 10, Prince William is expected to talk to Burnham about issues including homelessness, with both the prime minister and the prince committed to tackling the problem.

The two men have met before, such as the Omani state visit last month, where they both attended the state banquets at Windsor Castle.

But this is the first visit that Prince William has made to meet a serving prime minister in Downing Street - and the first senior royal to visit No 10 since the late Queen Elizabeth II came here in 2012.

Burnham has a weekly meeting with the prince's father, the King, and they are said to have developed a friendly relationship.

By convention, the Prince of Wales is meant to meet the prime minister once a year, but not necessarily at Downing Street. He met Sir Keir Starmer last year at Kensington Palace.

Prince William's appearance on a chilly morning will be seen as another step in his apprenticeship as a future king and head of state.

And it's expected that next year the prince will be carrying out more diplomatic visits at the request of the government.

The two men have a shared interest in addressing homelessness, which is expected to be among the topics under discussion.

Prince William has his Homewards project, which is testing ideas to reduce homelessness in six areas of the UK.

Burnham has pledged to give rough sleepers in England support to get off the streets by Christmas.

The prince and Andy Burnham have been active supporters of the Big Issue magazine which supports the homeless.

Both of the men have a reputation for being relaxed communicators in public, with Prince William recently getting plaudits for his unpompous appearance on the Graham Norton Show.

It's a relatively rare sight to see a royal in the prime minister's domain. The late Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1985 to commemorate the 250th anniversary of Downing Street and was here in 2012, when David Cameron was prime minister.

But there were no royal visitors during the intervening years, when Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer were prime ministers.

The then Prince Charles and Princess Diana visited 10 Downing Street in November 1989, for a dinner hosted by then then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher.

articles.title: Why Nato is worried about Russia's nuclear weapon in space
articles.summary: Russia's reported development of a nuclear anti-satellite weapon could fundamentally change the nature of warfare in space, threatening civilian satellite
articles.body: Russia's reported development of a nuclear anti-satellite weapon could fundamentally change the nature of warfare in space, threatening civilian satellite infrastructure, military communications and strategic early-warning systems. A nuclear explosion in orbit could damage or disable hundreds of satellites, disrupt navigation and communications networks and potentially trigger a military confrontation between nuclear powers on Earth.Nato chief Mark Rutte has warned that the alliance would respond to any threat to its assets in space, following reports that Russia was preparing to deploy a nuclear-armed satellite. Speaking at a press conference in Berlin, Rutte said Nato had several options at its disposal and would review its deterrence and defence posture if required. "When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, said he was unaware of the latest reports but dismissed claims based on unnamed sources, saying they were "hardly worth taking seriously".US intelligence agencies have been monitoring Russia's nuclear anti-satellite programme for almost a decade, according to the Berlin-based German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). Washington believes Moscow could eventually equip one or more satellites with nuclear warheads. The Russian satellite Cosmos 2553, launched in February 2022, has emerged as a central focus of these concerns, as per the same report. The spacecraft operates in an unusual orbital region, around 2,000 km above Earth, which is generally associated with decommissioned satellites.Moscow maintains that the satellite is intended to test the resilience of materials and electronic components under high-radiation conditions. However, the US government considers this explanation unconvincing, arguing that the radiation environment is insufficient to justify the stated purpose. Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, claims that Cosmos 2553 may carry a dummy warhead. The assessment, however, stresses that the satellite is not considered an operational anti-satellite weapon and does not currently pose an immediate threat.The potential deployment of a nuclear weapon in space would have consequences depending on the orbit selected. Low Earth Orbit (LEO), extending approximately 100 to 2,000 km above Earth, contains more than 90% of all satellites, including commercial communications and observation systems. Medium Earth Orbit (MEO), extending up to approximately 36,000 km, hosts important navigation constellations such as the American GPS, Europe's Galileo and Russia's GLONASS. Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO), beyond 36,000 km, contains weather, television and strategic military communications satellites, including systems supporting command and control and missile early-warning capabilities. A nuclear detonation in any of these orbital regions could therefore disrupt different layers of civilian and military infrastructure.Orbiting satellites can be neutralised or destroyed in four different ways: electronic warfare, cyber operations, kinetic weapons and non-kinetic weapons. Satellites are susceptible to electronic warfare by means of jamming and spoofing. This can be done by interfering with satellite signals or transmitting false information to receivers. Russia allegedly used GPS jamming in eastern Ukraine since 2014, while spoofing incidents in 2024 are said to have endangered civil aviation over Estonia.Cyberattacks have also been used to target satellite ground stations, in 2007 and 2008, an attack was carried out against American satellite ground stations. These two attacks were suspected to have been carried out by China. These cyber attacks demonstrate that hostile actors don't need space-based weapons to disrupt satellite operations.Kinetic anti-satellite weapons, on the other hand, include missiles launched from the ground to destroy satellites, as well as co-orbital systems positioned in space to approach and potentially interfere with other spacecraft. The United States, Russia, China and India have demonstrated direct-ascent anti-satellite capabilities by destroying their own defunct satellites. Russia also conducted a test in November 2021, destroying one of its own satellites and generating a substantial orbital cloud. China has demonstrated the ability to manoeuvre satellites close to other spacecraft, including a 2021 operation involving one of its decommissioned satellites.Non-kinetic weapons include high-powered lasers capable of dazzling or damaging satellite-based sensors. Even relatively low levels of laser energy can temporarily disrupt optical reconnaissance systems.A nuclear explosion in space, however, would be considerably more destructive than conventional anti-satellite weapons because its effects would extend beyond individual targets. The assessment identifies three principal consequences: an intense gamma-ray burst, increased radiation levels and an electromagnetic pulse (EMP). The gamma radiation could destroy satellites within approximately 80 km of the explosion, while fragments generated by the blast could damage spacecraft much farther away. As satellites move at very high speeds, even small pieces of debris could cause catastrophic damage on impact, potentially creating further debris and triggering a chain event; this is known as the Kessler effect or collisional cascading.The radiation effects could be equally damaging, as according to a US government study cited in the report, a relatively low-yield nuclear explosion of 10-20 kilotons in LEO could immediately affect between 5% and 10% of all satellites in space. Increased radiation levels could gradually damage onboard electronics, communications systems and satellite altitude-control mechanisms. An electromagnetic pulse (EMP) could also disrupt satellite electronics and may affect electrical infrastructure on Earth. Although the explosion would not directly threaten human life.Protecting satellites against such an event would be extremely difficult, as radiation shielding and EMP protection would increase satellite weight and manufacturing costs. EMP hardening alone could increase satellite costs by an estimated 5-10%. Military satellites are generally better protected, but even they would remain vulnerable to the enormous debris field created by a nuclear explosion. The US government estimates that LEO could become unusable for approximately a year following such an event.The deployment of nuclear weapons in space would also undermine international arms control. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. Even positioning a nuclear-armed satellite in space would violate the treaty, irrespective of whether its warhead was ever detonated. The 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty separately prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space. Russia is a signatory to both agreements, but Moscow did not reaffirm the Outer Space Treaty in 2024.Growing dependence of militaries and economies on satellites has created a new vulnerability and Russia's reported nuclear anti-satellite programme could provide Moscow with a means to threaten NATO. The militarisation of space is moving beyond conventional satellite disruption towards capabilities that could endanger space-based infrastructure and increase the risk of escalation between nuclear powers.

articles.title: M5 Willow Man could be replaced with 'stunning' sculpture
articles.summary: The Willow Man, near the M5 in Bridgwater, Somerset, has drastically deteriorated.
articles.body:
A 26-year-old sculpture which has fallen into disrepair could be replaced with a "stunning" carnival alternative.

The Willow Man, near the M5 in Bridgwater, Somerset, has drastically deteriorated since the 40ft (12m) landmark was created in 2000.

Bridgwater Without Parish Council has voted in principle to tear down the remaining structure and replace it with a willow Squibber Man.

Councillor Gary Bond said the town already has a small willow sculpture of a squibber in its centre. "If you could make that ten times bigger than it is, that would look stunning," he added.

Squibbing forms part of the annual Bridgwater Carnival , with about 150 participants simultaneously igniting large fireworks, known as squibs, on poles.

Councillors said they hoped the work could be carried out within the next 12 to 18 months, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

"It would be an absolute travesty if we don't act on this.

"It's on Kingsdown, which is within our parish. It will be done by local people, and we'll have buy-in from the carnival clubs," Bond added.

Chairman Robbie Davies said he was keen to clear the vegetation around the base of the current sculpture to allow the remaining elements to be safely dismantled.

"We can organise the workforce, maybe get some of the local community involved to remove the willow," he added.

Somerset Council said it was unable to commit any funding to repairing or restoring the landmark, with a report in 2023 concluding it would cost up to £1m.

The original Willow Man required planning permission and councillor Diogo Rodrigues urged the parish council to apply as soon as possible.

"The time it takes planning applications to go through at the minute is quite long.

"If you're looking to maybe get something up this time next year, I don't think it's unrealistic," he added.

articles.title: Indian-origin man killed in multi-car crash in Arkansas; daughter in ICU as community raises funds for family
articles.summary: A 39-year-old Indian-origin man, Ashok Somasundaram, was killed in a road accident in Bentonville, Arkansas.
articles.body: A 39-year-old Indian-origin man, Ashok Somasundaram, was killed in a road accident in Bentonville, Arkansas. His two young children were traveling with him. Both of them were injured. According to the Arkansas State Police, the crash occurred on November 21 afternoon at the intersection of SW 14th Street and Tunbridge Drive. A driver allegedly ran a red light and struck another vehicle, which was then pushed into Somasundaram.Arkansas State Police identified the other driver as 22-year-old Javier Edgardo Reyes Orellana. According to witnesses cited by police, he was travelling at a high speed on SW 14th Street when he allegedly ran a red light and struck Ashok's vehicle. The impact sent Ashok's vehicle into an e-bike ridden by 39-year-old Jacob Staly, who died at the scene. Ashok was taken to Mercy Hospital in Rogers, where he later died from his injuries. The other driver remained hospitalized, police said.Somasundaram's nine-year-old daughter is in the ICU and his 4-year-old son suffered minor injuries.The Northwest Arkansas Indian community set up a fundraiser for the family. Calling Ashok a devoted father of two young children and a loving husband of Sathya Gopal, it said that his sudden death has left his family facing an enormous emotional and financial burden, with his wife now having to cope with the loss while caring for their injured children. The fundraiser has been seeking to raise $400,000 to help the family meet the expenses arising from the tragedy. The money will go towards the daughter's ongoing hospital treatment and recovery, Ashok's funeral and memorial expenses, and the family's everyday living costs. The fundraiser also described Ashok as someone who was always willing to help and support people around him, and appealed to the community to stand by his wife and children during this difficult period. As of November 24, the campaign had collected over $295,000 through around 4,000 donations, according to its GoFundMe page.The community has also announced a visitation for Ashok on Tuesday, November 24, from 4 pm to 6 pm CST at Nelson-Berna Funeral Home, 4520 N Crossover Road, Fayetteville, Arkansas.You use AI every day. articles.title: BBC and Netflix team up for new CBeebies hub on streamer
articles.summary: The limited trial will see a CBeebies hub on Netflix for the first time and will feature 24 programmes.
articles.body:
The BBC and Netflix are to launch a trial hub on the streaming service next month, featuring 24 CBeebies shows.

Programmes including Hey Duggee, Numberblocks and Teletubbies can be seen on a branded CBeebies hub on Netflix from 2 December.

The trial's aim is to test new ways for the flagship pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC is the UK's largest commissioner of children's content.

BBC iPlayer will remain the home for all CBeebies content. Some CBeebies shows such as Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix, but this is the first time they will have a home hub on the subscription streamer.

CBeebies shows will also be made available to Netflix members outside the UK in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios, with the aim of driving investment into children's content in the UK. The deal does not include China.

Netflix will also commit to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions, the BBC said.

BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips said the corporation is "always looking at how we can help more audiences discover" its content and brands.

"This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience," she added.

Anne Mensah, vice president of Netflix's UK content said the "unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids' programme makers".

She added: "We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love."

The news comes against the backdrop of big changes at the BBC.

The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach a £500m savings target.

The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The corporation also faces growing competition for audiences from streaming services, gaming, social media and YouTube.

articles.title: 2 arrested over suspected burglary at royal family’s Sandringham estate
articles.summary: Prince William and Princess Kate’s country home Anmer Hall has been broken into, police said. The Prince and Princess of Wales were not home, a source said.
articles.body: LONDON — Two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the royal family’s Sandringham estate, British police said Tuesday, after a reported break-in at the country home of Prince William and Princess Kate. Police responded to reports of “suspicious activity” at the address Monday evening, dispatching searches by police dogs, drones a helicopter. That resulted in two men being arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing, according to a statement from the Norfolk Constabulary, the local police authority. The property was unoccupied at the time of the incident, it added. The Sun newspaper first reported that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, one of the residences used by the heir to the British throne and his wife, nestled in the heart of the royals’ sprawling estate. Kensington Palace, which handles communications for William and Kate, said it would not comment publicly on security matters. A royal source told NBC News that the couple and their three children, George, Charlotte and Louis, were not there at the time. The Waleses’ main home is Forest Lodge in Windsor, where they moved for a “fresh start” in 2025 after the death of Queen Elizabeth II and Kate’s cancer diagnosis. Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom country house built in the early 1800s, entered the royals’ extensive property portfolio when it was bought in 1898 by Queen Victoria’s son, who would later become King Edward VII. It has been used by various royals over the years. And William and Kate often enjoy the residence for weekend breaks and holidays. The incident will sharpen an ongoing debate about royal security. William, as a “working royal,” receives 24-hour armed security. But his brother, Prince Harry, does not, having moved to California in 2020 and relinquished his regal duties. Harry is in a protracted battle with authorities in a bid to reinstate this arrangement, which he argues is necessary due to his high-profile position and history of serving in the armed forces in Afghanistan. This summer, Harry and his wife, Meghan, and their two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, moved back to Britain. In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. King Charles and Queen Camilla weren’t at Windsor Castle at the time. Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Elizabeth. In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the queen’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette. Hours after the break-in, William was meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Tuesday on the doorstep of No. 10 Downing St., where they are expected to discuss issues such as homelessness. Meanwhile Kate is set to feature in a 30-minute documentary, “Heal,” about her cancer diagnosis and remission. It will air on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on Peacock from Dec. 1.

articles.title: Fears over North Yorkshire tourist tax have grown, council says
articles.summary: In a letter to the mayor, North Yorkshire Council says it remains opposed to a visitor levy.
articles.body:
North Yorkshire Council has said it opposes the introduction of a tourist tax for visitors staying in the county, with its concerns only increasing as plans for the levy develop.

In a letter to Mayor of York and North Yorkshire David Skaith, the authority's deputy leader Mark Crane said the option of not introducing such a tax "must remain genuinely open".

Crane said his main concern was the potential for a "percentage-based levy with no national ceiling" to be introduced, which he said many in the tourism sector found "particularly difficult and unfair".

In response, Skaith said he was "committed" to addressing any concerns before a decision about a tourist tax was made.

Crane's letter comes after the Visitor Levy (England) Bill, which would give regional mayors the power to create a tourist tax on overnight stays, was introduced in parliament earlier this month.

Meanwhile, in September a report commissioned by Skaith recommended imposing a £1 per night tourist tax across York and North Yorkshire - a move which the report claimed could raise £26m for the region each year, which could be ring-fenced for tourism-related purposes.

Crane's letter stated that the announcement of legislation "does not establish the case for imposing another charge on visitors and another administrative burden on businesses already under considerable pressure".

"Our concerns have increased, not diminished, as the proposals have developed," it said.

Despite the council's opposition, it would "engage constructively" to protect businesses and communities, the letter said.

"Our engagement should not be mistaken for support or acceptance that a levy is inevitable," the letter added.

In response, a spokesperson for Skaith said: "Residents across York and North Yorkshire have to live with, and pay for, the additional pressures that the high number of visitors place on our county's public services.

"It is only fair to ask them to contribute towards those costs and enable us to invest in our towns, cities and villages to make them even more attractive to tourists."

The spokesperson added that a full public consultation and impact assessment would be carried out and engagement with the tourism sector would continue.

"The mayor is not content with the continued lack of investment into the things that matter most to residents, like transport and making our high streets the best they can be," they said.

"He will always put our county, and its residents, first."

articles.title: Ten years after its 2016 peace deal, Colombia faces a return to conflict
articles.summary: Critics fear that a security crackdown under Abelardo de la Espriella could unravel gains made under the 2016 deal.
articles.body:
Bogota, Colombia – Ten years ago, Jorge Suarez and more than 13,000 other fighters agreed to a peace treaty with the Colombian government, paving the way for the disarmament of Latin America’s largest rebel group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).

“It was an agreement that I never thought would happen,” Suarez told Al Jazeera.

Born in a rebel camp, he had been fighting since the age of 15. But on November 24, 2016, an agreement signed paved the way for Suarez and other FARC members to lay down their arms.

The deal was historic. It was the culmination of more than four years of negotiations and earned Colombia's president at the time, Juan Manuel Santos, the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts.

But Colombia's six-decade-long internal armed conflict has continued in the years since. Armed groups, new and old, have continued to clash with government forces. Illegal mining and a booming cocaine trade have fuelled the fighting.

Colombia has also turned away from negotiated solutions to the conflict.

In June, the country elected far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella, who pledged to restore security through military force rather than peace talks.

Now, on the 10th anniversary of the peace deal, those involved reflect on what went wrong, what worked, and whether the country can overcome its deep-seated divisions.

articles.title: Thousands raised for George the Stourbridge station cat's vet bills
articles.summary: George is receiving veterinary care and is due to undergo scans, his social media manager says.
articles.body:
More than £40,000 has been raised to help pay for a popular railway station cat's vet bills after he suddenly fell ill.

George, the Stourbridge Junction cat, was receiving treatment and had spent the night at a veterinary clinic after becoming "very poorly", a post on Facebook said on Monday.

The beloved ginger-and-white feline became an online sensation for regularly hanging around the station, amassing more than 260,000 followers across various social media platforms.

In an update Simone Carter - his very own social media manager - said George had been placed on a drip and was undergoing scans to find out what was wrong.

"I've just had an update from George's dad... he's doing okay," she said.

"His kidneys and liver function are all good. His thyroid's slightly raised."

Carter explained the famous train cat was taken to vets on Monday after his owners noticed a "bit of a decline in him", where he was eating less and sleeping more than usual over the weekend .

The cat, who has his own marker on Google Maps , first started popping into Stourbridge Junction in 2017 and was adopted by the staff when his owner emigrated to Spain.

The 12-year-old feline has since become something of a local celebrity, attracting fans from as far afield as the United States, Canada and Asia.

A book about his life was also published earlier this year.

"He's loved by a lot of people, you know, he's more than just a station cat for a lot of people," Carter said.

"He's part of their daily routine, he brings a little bit of happiness, companionship, and comfort, especially for those who are going through a rough time, and a little bit of cheekiness as well."

Carter told BBC Radio WM any money remaining after George's veterinary bills were paid would go to other animal charities.

"I've set up a separate bank account just for George's funds," she said.

"So once we've paid what we need to for his vet bills, then we can look at assisting animal charities, cat charities, you know, both locally and further afield, so this will benefit so many rescues."

She added she was keeping in contact with the much-loved feline's dad and would provide further updates on his social media pages.

"Everybody is just so terribly concerned about this lovely little boy," she said.

"He's a little ray of sunshine in a corner of the internet."

articles.title: Walking Dead artist creates image for Shrewsbury pizza business
articles.summary: Dough and Oil has taken over the building where zombie artist Charlie Adlard's family once had a shop.
articles.body:
Did you hear the one about zombies in need of a quick bite? If not, a takeaway in Shrewsbury can fill you in.

Its pizza boxes feature an image of the undead getting a bit peckish - but the artwork is not via any old sketcher of the scary skulkers, it's direct from the pen of Charlie Adlard, who drew The Walking Dead comics on which the hit TV series was based.

But why mix the munchies with his take on moaning monsters? It's all to do with Adlard's personal history with the premises.

The takeaway operates from a building once run as a tobacconist shop by Adlard's family.

Adlard & Son in Shrewsbury was opened by his grandmother in 1943 and was later passed down to his father. It closed in 2021.

The ground floor has now re-opened as a takeaway service from restaurant Dough and Oil which was already established elsewhere in the town, and the owners have been keen to recognise the building's link to the celebrated artist.

"Me doing some artwork for a pizza box was the obvious sort of thing to connect the two," Adlard told the BBC.

He came up with an image based on published art from the 50th issue of the comic and features someone eating a slice while the hands of the undead grab towards it.

Adlard described it as "a guy eating a pizza in the corner. giving it the Scooby Doo face".

He said it made sense that it was "slightly comical rather than horror".

"You don't want to scare your pizza customers away do you?" he explained.

Adlard remembered his grandmother as a "very powerful lady" who always smoked a cigarette in a cigarette holder.

Back in the 1940s he said it would have been unusual for a woman to own a business and "you didn't meddle with her".

His father took it over in the 1950s and said his early memories of the shop were helping out there in the school holidays.

As he grew older, he said his father got him to do the lettering for the signs.

"I didn't do drawings or anything, but I was always obviously the best letterer in the family," he said.

"So my artwork, in inverted commas, did appear in the shop window on a very, very regular basis.

"Then I escaped to art college and he couldn't get me anymore."

Despite being the son of a tobacconist, he said: "The irony is I've never smoked.

"When I was at school, [I] tried one or two [cigarettes], but hated it and that's it."

Adlard's father retired at the age of 60 and the business passed to new owners, while keeping its name.

When it was bought by Dough and Oil, Adlard was invited back in to look around, and said the latest transformation took him by surprise, especially the work that had been done to the cellar, which is now a store room and office.

He said: "I remember the cellar when my dad was there and it was just the worst, most dank, horrible, creepy place you could possibly imagine.

"You went down these rickety stairs at the back and it was properly under the street and you could see the people's feet, you know, from the grill up into the street and it was cobwebs everywhere."

Adlard was also asked to donated a photo of his father standing proudly outside the shop doorway, which will decorate the business.

He said that had been "a nice touch" and he planned to do a full-colour version of his pizza box image to hang on its wall.

"Hopefully I'll be able to go in there and play the 'do you know who I am?' card for a long time coming," he said.

articles.title: Steps on to table Ratna Bhandar keys probe report in assembly: CM
articles.summary: Odisha CM Mohan Charan Majhi says steps are underway to table the Justice Raghubir Das report on Ratna Bhandar missing keys in the assembly.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi has said the state govt is taking steps to comply with the Orissa high court’s direction to table the Justice Raghubir Das Commission report on missing keys of Puri Jagannath Temple’s Ratna Bhandar in the assembly.In a written reply to a question by suspended BJD MLA Arvind Mohapatra on whether the high court’s directive was not complied with, Majhi said on Monday, “The high court had directed the govt on Jan 27 to place the commission report before the assembly. Necessary steps are being taken to comply with the court’s direction.”According to govt sources, the report is likely to be placed before the cabinet before being tabled in the assembly.The mystery surrounding the missing keys surfaced after a govt-appointed team failed to open the inner chamber of Ratna Bhandar on April 4, 2018 owing to unavailability of the keys.The previous govt formed a judicial commission headed by Justice Raghubir Das on June 6, 2018, to probe circumstances under which the original keys went missing. The commission submitted its report to the govt on Nov 29 that year.The Ratna Bhandar issue emerged as a major poll plank for the BJP ahead of the 2024 assembly elections, with the party promising to reopen the treasury for inventory and make the inquiry report on the missing keys public.After winning the elections, the BJP govt reopened Ratna Bhandar on July 14, 2024. articles.title: States sue HUD over rule that could cut off housing aid for mixed immigration status families
articles.summary: The 21 states and Pennsylvania’s governor say the rule could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing.
articles.body: Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania’s governor have sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to families if any household member lacks eligible citizenship or immigration status. The states say the rule could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing. States including California, New York, Arizona and Massachusetts joined the suit. HUD defends the rule, arguing illegal immigrants are taking advantage of the current eligibility requirements. The rule takes effect on Dec. 14. It would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance. “No child should lose their home over a parent’s immigration status,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. “This rule is cruel, and it’s unlawful.” For over three decades, Congress has authorized prorated federal housing assistance for mixed-status families, whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. These families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status. The new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any assistance. “Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home,” Bonta said. One in five children in California is part of a mixed-status family, said Bonta, estimating that the rule will affect 7,000 households in his state. The new rule would also require public housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. “Congress never gave HUD the power to throw mixed-status families out of their homes or turn private landlords into immigration enforcement. But that’s exactly what this rule does,” Bonta said. The new rule is the latest in a series of moves by President Donald Trump’s administration targeting legal immigrants. Those moves include restricting healthcare, nutrition benefits and other subsidies while stripping legal protections from some immigrant groups to make more people eligible for deportation. HUD Secretary Scott Turner first announced the proposed rule in January, but the department finalized it only last week. “HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist,” said Turner in an emailed statement on Monday. Earlier this year, HUD conducted an audit with DHS and identified 20,000 mixed-status households receiving federally funded housing assistance nationwide. The department said illegal immigrants were using “loopholes” to access benefits while the department struggled to provide housing for all who need it.

articles.title: 7 Andhra Pradesh fishermen missing after boat loses contact near Odisha's Paradip coast
articles.summary: KAKINADA: As many as seven fishermen from Uppada in Kakinada district have gone missing after the motorised fishing boat they were travelling in lost
articles.body: KAKINADA: As many as seven fishermen from Uppada in Kakinada district have gone missing after the motorised fishing boat they were travelling in lost contact near Paradip Port in Odisha.The fishermen had ventured into the sea on November 4, and there has been no communication from the boat since November 19.Chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu spoke with officials to inquire about the missing fishing boat and the measures being taken to trace it. He directed officials to intensify search operations and provide regular updates to the families of the missing fishermen.Immediately after receiving information about the incident, search operations were launched in coordination with Coast Guard officials in Kakinada, Chennai and Odisha.The Kakinada District Fisheries Department also wrote to the Indian Coast Guard seeking assistance in tracing the boat.Officials said the mobile phones of the missing fishermen and the boat's transponder were switched off. Efforts to trace the vessel through GPS have also failed. The Indian Coast Guard is conducting search operations along the Paradip coast with the help of ships and a helicopter.The boat departed from Subbam Peta in Uppada mandal on November 4. Boat owner Garikina Simhadri reportedly informed his brother, Garikina Tatababu, that the crew would venture into the deep sea for fishing and might not be within mobile network coverage.District fisheries officer V Krishna Rao told The Times of India that two boats had left Uppada on November 4 and subsequently ventured into the sea from Visakhapatnam. While one boat returned on November 18, the owner of the missing boat had informed the crew of the returning vessel that they intended to venture farther into the sea.The missing boat was last spotted in the vicinity of Paradip Port before contact was lost. Krishna Rao said the vessel had approximately 1,500 litres of fuel and sufficient provisions for a month. He expressed hope that the boat might have travelled around 200 nautical miles beyond Paradip and would return safely.The district fisheries officer is in continuous contact with the Coast Guard stations at Paradip and Kakinada, the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Chennai and the fishermen's families. The Coast Guard at Paradip has been conducting aerial surveillance and deploying ships to locate the missing vessel.Meanwhile, deputy chief minister Pawan Kalyan spoke with the Kakinada district collector over the phone to obtain details of the incident and the ongoing search operations.The collector informed him that officials had been in contact with the fishermen's families until November 14, after which communication ceased. However, enquiries revealed that the boat had been spotted near Paradip Port until November 18.The collector said search operations were initiated immediately after the information was received, and Coast Guard officials in Kakinada, Chennai and Odisha were contacted for assistance. A search operation was also conducted with the help of a Navy helicopter.
